It covers users, roles, granular permissions, sessions, and CSRF protection out of the box.

| Piece | Responsibility |
|-------|----------------|
| **Auth** | Login, logout, session lifecycle |
| **PermissionManager** | Resolves what a user is allowed to do, and on which records — see [Permissions](/permissions) |
| **ActionScanner** | Discovers controller actions and their access rules |
| **CSRF** | Cross-site request forgery protection |
| **Two-factor** | Authenticator-app codes (TOTP) on every login path |

Passwords are never stored in plain text — Loopar hashes them with **Argon2** via `loopar.hash(plain)`.

For the framework-wide picture — tenant isolation, secret fields, headers, uploads, rate limits — see [Security](/security).
"}}]}, {"element": "div", "data": {"label": "Users & Sessions", "key": "auth_sessions", "id": "auth_sessions", "name": "auth_sessions"}, "elements": [{"element": "title", "data": {"key": "title_auth_sessions", "text": "Users & Sessions", "size": "md", "id": "title_auth_sessions", "name": "title_auth_sessions", "label": "Title auth_sessions"}}, {"element": "markdown", "data": {"key": "md_auth_sessions", "value": "## The Current User

Server-side code reads the authenticated user through `loopar.currentUser` (or `null` when the request is anonymous):

```javascript
import { loopar } from "loopar";

const user = loopar.currentUser;

if (!user) {
  loopar.throw({ code: 401, message: "Authentication required" });
}

console.log(user.name, user.email, user.user_type);
```

> `loopar.session` is a per-request key/value store (`get`/`set`/`remove`) used for things like list filters — it is **not** the user object.

## Looking Up Users

User helpers live on `loopar.auth`:

```javascript
// Fetch a user by id or email
const user = await loopar.auth.getUser("user@example.com");

// Check whether an account is disabled
const disabled = await loopar.auth.disabledUser(userId);
```

## Login & Logout

Authentication is handled by the framework's `Auth` layer. A successful login sets an httpOnly **JWT cookie** (`loopar_token_<tenant>`, 1-day expiry, auto-refreshed near expiration) plus a readable CSRF cookie; logout clears them. You normally don't call these directly — the built-in auth pages and API routes do. When the user has two-factor authentication on, the session is opened only after the code step (see below)."}}]}, {"element": "div", "data": {"label": "OAuth Social Login", "key": "auth_oauth", "id": "auth_oauth", "name": "auth_oauth"}, "elements": [{"element": "title", "data": {"key": "title_auth_oauth", "id": "title_auth_oauth", "name": "title_auth_oauth", "text": "OAuth Social Login", "size": "2xl"}}, {"element": "markdown", "data": {"key": "md_auth_oauth", "name": "md_auth_oauth", "value": "Loopar supports social login with **Google** and **GitHub** out of the box (OAuth 2.0; PKCE for Google). When a provider is configured, "Continue with..." buttons appear automatically on the login form.

## Configuration

Two ways, per provider — the **Oauth Settings** entity takes precedence over env vars:

**Option A — Oauth Settings entity** (Desk → Auth):

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `provider` | `google` or `github` |
| `client_id` / `client_secret` | From the provider's console |
| `scopes` | Optional, space/comma separated (sane defaults per provider) |
| `enabled` | Turn the provider on |
| `allow_signup` | Create a user on first verified login |

**Option B — environment variables** (fallback when no enabled entity row exists):

```bash
OAUTH_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=...
OAUTH_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET=...
OAUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID=...
OAUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET=...
OAUTH_GOOGLE_ALLOW_SIGNUP=1     # optional
OAUTH_BASE_URL=https://mysite.com   # optional, overrides the derived base URL
```

Set the provider's **redirect URI** to `https://<your-domain>/auth/oauthCallback`.

## The Flow

```
GET /auth/oauth?provider=google
  → signed 10-min transaction cookie (state + PKCE verifier)
  → redirect to the provider

GET /auth/oauthCallback?code=...&state=...
  → validate state, exchange code, fetch profile
  → require verified email
  → link or create the user → login (or the two-factor code step)
```

Failures bounce back to `/auth/login?oauth=<reason>` (e.g. `not_configured`, `email_unverified`, `not_member`, `disabled`, `mfa_locked`).

## Account Linking

1. **Stable identity first:** a user is matched by `(oauth_provider, oauth_sub)` — so it survives email changes.
2. **Email bridge:** on first social login, a user with the same verified email gets the OAuth identity anchored to their account.
3. **Signup:** unknown identity + `allow_signup` → a new `Web` user is created (random password, provider picture as avatar). Without `allow_signup`, the login is rejected (`not_member`).

Secrets never reach the browser: the login form only asks `POST /auth/oauthProviders`, which returns provider names and labels."}}]}, {"element": "div", "data": {"label": "Two-Factor Authentication", "key": "auth_mfa", "id": "auth_mfa", "name": "auth_mfa"}, "elements": [{"element": "title", "data": {"key": "title_auth_mfa", "text": "Two-Factor Authentication", "size": "md", "id": "title_auth_mfa", "name": "title_auth_mfa", "label": "Title auth_mfa"}}, {"element": "markdown", "data": {"key": "md_auth_mfa", "name": "md_auth_mfa", "value": "Any user can add a second factor to their account: a 6-digit code from an authenticator app. It is standard **TOTP** (RFC 6238), so it works with Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, 1Password, Authy, Bitwarden and the rest.

## Turning It On

**Profile → Security → Turn on two-factor authentication**:

1. Scan the QR code with the app (or type the key shown under it).
2. Enter the first code. This proves the app works — only then is 2FA switched on.
3. Save the **10 recovery codes**. Each one works once, and they are shown only this time.

From the same panel the user can generate new recovery codes or turn 2FA off. Both ask for a current code.

## Signing In

With 2FA on, **every** login path stops before the session is opened — password, Google/GitHub and the cloud claim link alike:

```
login (any path) → challenge: signed 5-minute cookie, no session yet
                 → code step: POST /auth/mfaVerify { code } or { recovery_code }
                 → session opened (JWT carries mfa: true)
```

The login form shows the code step by itself, inside the modal or on the full page. After an OAuth popup or a full-page redirect it resumes at `/auth/login?mfa=1`.

| Protection | Rule |
|------------|------|
| One-time codes | A code is accepted once; replaying it inside its 30-second window fails |
| Clock drift | One 30-second step either way is tolerated |
| Per challenge | 5 wrong codes and the user goes back to the password step |
| Per user | 10 failures in 15 minutes block the code step until the window passes — a new password login doesn't reset it |
| Per IP | The code step shares the auth rate limit (15 requests / 15 minutes) |
| At rest | Secret encrypted (AES-256-GCM, per-tenant key); recovery codes hashed (Argon2) |

## Lost Phone

- **Recovery code** — "Use a recovery code" on the code step.
- **An administrator** — Desk → User → **Reset 2FA**. Needs the `resetMfa` grant on `User` (Administrator always has it).
- **The server** — the way back in for the Administrator itself:

```bash
yarn mfa-reset <tenant> <user>
```

## Custom Login Flows

If an app adds its own way to sign in (a magic link, an SSO provider), open the session with `completeLogin(user)` from the auth module's `mfa.js` instead of calling `loopar.auth.login(user)` directly. `completeLogin` returns `{ session }`, `{ mfa_required }` or `{ mfa_locked }`; calling `login()` yourself skips the second factor."}}]}, {"element": "div", "data": {"label": "Roles & Permissions", "key": "auth_permissions", "id": "auth_permissions", "name": "auth_permissions"}, "elements": [{"element": "title", "data": {"key": "title_auth_permissions", "text": "Roles & Permissions", "size": "md", "id": "title_auth_permissions", "name": "title_auth_permissions", "label": "Title auth_permissions"}}, {"element": "markdown", "data": {"key": "md_auth_permissions", "value": "Loopar's authorization model is **role-based with per-document grants and record-level ownership**. It is documented in full on the [Permissions](/permissions) page; this is the one-paragraph version.

| Level | Example |
|-------|---------|
| **Document · action** | Who may `update` an `Invoice` |
| **Scope** | All invoices, or only the ones the user created (`own`) |
| **App / wildcard** | Everything in the `sales` app (`App:sales`), every `list` (`*:list`) |
| **Deny** | Block one action for one user regardless of roles |

Roles are seeded by apps (`<App> Manager`, `<App> User`, plus `static roles` in the installer); the admin refines them in **Desk → Auth → Role Permission Manager**.

## Checking Permissions

```javascript
import { PermissionManager } from "loopar";

PermissionManager.can("Customer", "delete", username);    // boolean — allowed at all?
PermissionManager.scope("Customer", "update", username);  // 'all' | 'own' | null
PermissionManager.getPermissions(username);               // snapshot sent to the client

await PermissionManager.reload(username);                 // re-read after writing grants outside the ORM
```

Ownership (`scope: own`) is checked per request on `__created_by__` — or on the column your controller declares with `static ownerField`. Details, module visibility and the client helpers (`award`, `scope`, `canOn`) are on the [Permissions](/permissions) page.
"}}]}, {"element": "div", "data": {"label": "Controller Actions & Access", "key": "auth_actions", "id": "auth_actions", "name": "auth_actions"}, "elements": [{"element": "title", "data": {"key": "title_auth_actions", "text": "Controller Actions & Access", "size": "md", "id": "title_auth_actions", "name": "title_auth_actions", "label": "Title auth_actions"}}, {"element": "markdown", "data": {"key": "md_auth_actions", "value": "Only methods prefixed with `action` or `publicAction` on a controller are reachable over HTTP. Everything else stays private to the server.

```javascript
import { BaseController } from "loopar";

export default class InvoiceController extends BaseController {
  // Reachable: POST /Invoice/approve (loopar.call) — requires login + permission
  async actionApprove() { /* ... */ }

  // Reachable WITHOUT login (publicAction): POST /Invoice/webhook — or /api/Invoice/webhook for third parties
  async publicActionWebhook() { /* ... */ }

  // NOT reachable over HTTP — internal helper only
  recalcTotals() { /* ... */ }
}
```

`ActionScanner` walks every app and registers these actions so `PermissionManager` can guard them. Unauthenticated actions are surfaced through `ActionScanner.getPublicActions()`.

## Where Permissions Are Enforced

Permission checks run at the **HTTP action layer** (before your `action*` method executes): first the action grant, then — for `own`-scoped grants — ownership of the requested record. Lists of the requested document are narrowed the same way; see [Permissions](/permissions). Server-side code that isn't dispatched through a controller — model hooks, installers, scheduled jobs — is trusted and writes directly:

```javascript
// No permission check here; this is trusted server code
const doc = await loopar.getDocument("Invoice", name);
doc.status = "Approved";
await doc.save();
```

`publicAction*` methods skip login, permission and CSRF checks entirely — validate their input carefully."}}]}, {"element": "div", "data": {"label": "CSRF & Realtime", "key": "auth_csrf", "id": "auth_csrf", "name": "auth_csrf"}, "elements": [{"element": "title", "data": {"key": "title_auth_csrf", "text": "CSRF & Realtime", "size": "md", "id": "title_auth_csrf", "name": "title_auth_csrf", "label": "Title auth_csrf"}}, {"element": "markdown", "data": {"key": "md_auth_csrf", "value": "## CSRF Protection

Loopar uses the **double-submit cookie** pattern. On login the server sets a readable `csrf-token` cookie; every state-changing request (non-GET) on an authenticated workspace (`desk`, `api`, `portal`) must echo it back in the `x-csrf-token` header. The framework's client does this automatically; validation runs before the request reaches your controller. `GET` requests and `publicAction*` methods are exempt.

## Realtime Authentication

Loopar's realtime layer (Socket.IO) authenticates connections with the same **JWT cookie**, scoped to the tenant namespace — a socket for tenant A cannot join tenant B's rooms, so realtime events respect the same tenant isolation as the rest of the framework."}}]}, {"element": "div", "data": {"label": "Best Practices", "key": "auth_best", "id": "auth_best", "name": "auth_best"}, "elements": [{"element": "title", "data": {"key": "title_auth_best", "text": "Best Practices", "size": "md", "id": "title_auth_best", "name": "title_auth_best", "label": "Title auth_best"}}, {"element": "markdown", "data": {"key": "md_auth_best", "value": "- **Never expose the dev site publicly** — it is the admin control center for every tenant.
- **Turn on two-factor authentication for desk users**, starting with Administrator.
- **Prefer `doc.save()`** over `loopar.db.setValue()` when validation and model hooks matter — the low-level DB API bypasses the model lifecycle.
- **Use `action*` for authenticated operations and reserve `publicAction*` for genuinely public endpoints** — public actions skip login, permission and CSRF checks.
- **Hash secrets with `loopar.hash()`** (Argon2) — never store credentials or tokens in plain text.
- **Scope realtime events** to the tenant namespace; don't broadcast across tenants."}}]}]}]
